column4: Immediately after being confronted with “this report” in 53:59, the hearers laugh rather than weep; their reaction reverses the humbled, tearful reception that the section's news calls for.
The passage about the audience's response to “this report” ends by commanding prostration and worship, supplying the bodily humility appropriate to what has been heard.
After 56:81 asks why the audience treats “this report” lightly, this ayah identifies denial as their return for divine provision, making the hearer's response explicit.
The jinn say the Quran they heard guides to right conduct, so they believe in it; this states what happens when the heard revelation becomes understanding and obedience.
The jinn say that when they heard the guidance they believed, a direct formula for سماع producing the receptive response the section distinguishes from bare audition.
When God's signs are recited, believers' faith increases; the arriving words alter their hearers instead of passing through as mere sound.
Believers are told to obey God and the Messenger and not turn away while they are hearing, directly joining audition to the obedience included in سماع.
The believers say they heard a caller calling to faith and consequently believed, an explicit chain from heard proclamation to response.
When God's signs are recited, the arrogant person turns away as though he had not heard and as though his ears were blocked, dramatizing hearing without reception.
The sinner hears God's signs recited yet persists arrogantly as if he had not heard them, another exact boundary between sound reaching the ear and meaningful listening.
God has heard the woman disputing with the Prophet and complaining to Him, and He hears their dialogue; a human utterance reaches the divine Hearer and becomes revealed report.
At the Fire, people's hearing, sight, and skins testify against them; the faculty that once received warning becomes a speaker in the final account.
They ask their skins why they testified, and the skins answer that God made them speak; ordinary control of voice is reversed in the Judgment scene.
On the Day, tongues, hands, and feet testify about what people did, showing that final testimony sounds even when defendants cannot control their own account.
The Book is sent to the Prophet so he may warn with it and as a reminder for believers, combining first reception, proclamation, and remembrance.
The revelation is “only a reminder to the worlds,” extending the received message beyond its first addressee to every later audience.
The Prophet asks no payment for the message, which is only a reminder to the worlds; his role is transmission rather than control or gain.
The proclamation is only a reminder to the worlds, giving the report the same outward movement implied when the first hearer becomes a reminder.
The Quran is only a reminder to the worlds, directly defining the “report” by its work in successive hearers.
The recitation is only a reminder to the worlds, another repeated formulation of the message passing beyond its first recipient.
After accounts of earlier prophets, “this is a reminder” turns the just-narrated stories into present moral recollection for the audience.
The question “how can reminder benefit them?” is answered by the fact that a clear messenger already came and was rejected, making later recognition too late.
The regretful person says a companion led him away from the Reminder after it had come to him, directly joining arrival of the message to failed retention.
The question whether messengers bear anything beyond clear conveyance repeats the exact limit on the reminder's authority.
Although the Prophet's people deny the true message, he says he is not a trustee over them, separating the delivered report from control of its hearers.
After insights have come from God, seeing or remaining blind belongs to each person, and the Prophet is not their guardian; reception remains the listener's responsibility.
God has not made the Prophet a guardian or trustee over the idolaters, closely paralleling the boundary following 88:21's command to remind.
Truth has come from the Lord, but each person bears the result of guidance or error and the Prophet is not their trustee.
God knows the audience best and has not sent the Prophet as their trustee, limiting the human speaker while leaving judgment to God.
God sends the Book to the Prophet for humankind in truth, but the Prophet is not a trustee over those who choose error; received revelation and limited authority appear together.
God is guardian over those who take other protectors, while the Prophet is not their trustee, preserving the same division between reminder and divine oversight.
Whoever obeys the Messenger obeys God, but if people turn away the Prophet has not been sent as their guardian.
God tells the Prophet that He relates some news of the ruined towns, making their former response into warning heard by a new audience.
“This is from the news of the towns which We relate to you” explicitly turns surviving and harvested settlements into revealed narrative for the Prophet.
The addressee is commanded to listen for the Day when the caller calls from a near place, carrying the section's address to the final sound itself.
On that Day people hear the Cry in truth and emerge, specifying what the commanded listening of 50:41 anticipates.
The Prophet is told to turn from rejecters until the Day the caller summons them to something terrible, setting the call that draws the humbled eyes of 54:7.
People hasten toward the caller and unbelievers name it a hard Day, completing the summoned, humbled procession begun in 54:6–7.
After saying the Prophet cannot make the dead or deaf hear, the passage says he makes only believers who submit hear, defining effective hearing positively.
The Prophet can make only believers who submit hear, completing 27:80's limit with the identity of receptive listeners.
No town is destroyed without warners having reached it, so becoming a ruined example follows a prior opportunity to hear.
The warners serve as reminder and God does not wrong the town, explaining why delivered warning precedes the cautionary history of 26:208.
God does not destroy towns until a messenger in their center recites His signs to them; judged peoples first become hearers of warning.
God declares that He has sent down a reminder to the audience, presenting ذكر itself as something that arrives from above.
A messenger recites God's clear signs to bring believers from darkness to light, specifying the human voice through which the reminder of 65:10 reaches them.
The Prophet is commanded to say, “It is tremendous news,” another direct designation of the warning proclamation as eschatological news.
The audience turns away from the tremendous news named in 38:67, making failed reception rather than lack of delivery the problem.
When the signs are recited, rejecters say they have already heard and dismiss them as tales of the ancients, misclassifying true revelation as disposable old story.
The transgressor answers recited signs with “tales of the ancients,” reversing the section's use of true past reports as revelation and reminder.
People in Paradise turn to one another asking questions, confirming from another Garden passage that absence of vain speech does not mean absence of meaningful conversation.
The rejecters see the promised event as remote, giving the audience's temporal stance that the already-arrived form of the section's report corrects.
God sees the promised event as near, reversing the distance assigned to it by the hearers in 70:6.
Abraham asks for a truthful tongue or honorable mention among later peoples, a positive reversal of condemned communities becoming cautionary reports.
God grants Abraham and his family an exalted truthful mention among later people, showing a blessed form of becoming remembered speech.
The hearers remain heedlessly preoccupied after 53:59 confronts them with the report; the ayah contributes the inattentive stance between laughter and the command to prostrate.
No private counsel escapes God's presence, and He will inform its speakers on Resurrection Day; speech unheard by other people still becomes final disclosure.
Whether speech is voiced aloud or kept secret, God knows the secret and what is still more hidden, setting a divine boundary around “unheard” words.
God knows how opponents listen to the Prophet and what they say in private counsel, bringing public hearing and concealed hostile speech into one scene.
The Prophet must tell God's servants to say what is best because Satan sows discord through speech, an earthly discipline corresponding to Paradise's purified words.
Good words ascend to God and righteous action raises them, giving morally sound speech a destination and weight unlike vain utterance.
Believers are commanded to avoid false speech, a specific earthly prohibition on the kind of corrupt utterance excluded from the Garden.
Those who forget God are made to forget themselves, extending the section's opposition between reminder and forgetting to loss of self-knowledge.
Satan makes his party forget God's remembrance, naming the force by which a received reminder can be displaced.
Amid demands placed on revelation, the Prophet is told he is only a warner while God is trustee over everything, limiting his role to proclamation.
The Prophet cannot guide even whom he loves; God gives effective guidance, another boundary between speaking the reminder and producing its result.
Some messengers' accounts are related to the Prophet and others are not, explicitly presenting prophetic history as selected revealed report.
The Prophet is commanded to warn of the approaching Day when hearts choke in throats, bringing the still-future scene near through present speech.
The Prophet is told not to move his tongue hastily with the revelation, a precise glimpse of the first recipient preparing to voice what he receives.
The revelation comes in a clear Arabic tongue, supplying the linguistic form of the warning placed on the Prophet's heart in 26:194.
At one call from God, people emerge from the earth, a concise counterpart to the Judgment procession following its caller.
On the Day God calls, people respond with praise and realize how briefly they remained, showing the final call producing unavoidable response.
Noah's people are drowned after denying the messengers and made a sign for humankind, a nonlexical instance of failed hearers becoming later warning.

هَلْ أَتَىٰ opens with the same interrogative arrival formula, but asks about a time that passed over humanity before it was a thing mentioned; it offers a formal and temporal counterpoint to news arriving to the Prophet.
